structure.title: Chapters 1–12 · Netherfield is let
structure.text: A house acquires a rich tenant and within hours Mrs Bennet has a husband in mind for one of her daughters. An assembly gives the neighbourhood its first look at the newcomers. Elizabeth overhears what Darcy thinks of dancing with her and finds, in telling the story afterwards, that an insult can be rather good fun.

structure.title: Chapters 13–26 · A visitor who will inherit the house
structure.text: Mr Collins arrives with apologies, compliments and a proposal for making everyone comfortable. While Elizabeth is congratulating herself on seeing through him, her friend Charlotte has to consider the same man from another position. Two intelligent women with a taste for the same jokes can find very different things bearable in a husband.

structure.title: Chapters 27–45 · Kent and Derbyshire change the evidence
structure.text: Away from her own neighbourhood, Elizabeth encounters letters, relatives, servants and houses able to tell her things the local assembly could not. Austen gives a change of mind an exact geography. A person can travel far enough to hear another account of the man she thought she knew.

people.name: Elizabeth Bennet
people.role: A witty daughter confident in her judgment
people.text: Elizabeth enjoys recognising absurdity and refusing to be overawed by wealth. Her intelligence is a pleasure to follow. It also gives her persuasive ways to defend an opinion she likes, especially when a story rewards her confidence in herself.

people.name: Fitzwilliam Darcy
people.role: A wealthy visitor with guarded manners
people.text: Darcy arrives with social advantages he has little need to explain. His reserve gives other people ample material for interpretation. The novel gradually makes the difference between someone's manners, motives, and conduct harder to settle through one encounter.

people.name: Jane Bennet and Charles Bingley
people.text: Jane's readiness to think well of people and Bingley's sociability make their attachment seem relatively straightforward. Yet private feeling develops among relatives and friends who can interpret, encourage, or discourage it. Good intentions do not give either person complete knowledge of the other.

people.name: Charlotte Lucas
people.text: Charlotte can agree with Elizabeth about what is ridiculous without sharing her freedom to dismiss it. Their friendship makes room for a difficult comparison between a choice made under constraint and the same choice viewed from a more hopeful position.

context.title: The house will not belong to the daughters
context.text: The Bennet estate is entailed away from the female line. Their father's death would therefore change the women's home and income as well as their family life. Mrs Bennet's anxiety about marriage is often ridiculous in expression, but the problem she is trying to solve is real.

passages.quote: a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.

context.title: Politeness carries information without settling it
context.text: An invitation, a dance, or a visit can suggest interest without declaring an intention. People must read such signals while knowing that rank, convenience, and ordinary courtesy may produce similar behaviour. Austen's misunderstandings grow within these real limits on what can be openly asked.

context.title: The narrator can sound like the person being examined
context.text: Austen sometimes lets a character's assumptions shape the narration without placing the words inside quotation marks. The resulting sentence can feel authoritative and still invite doubt. This makes the act of reading resemble the characters' own problem of deciding whose judgment deserves confidence.

notice.text: Notice how much evidence an agreeable speaker needs.
notice.why: Someone who confirms an existing dislike may receive a welcome that a less flattering account would not. Follow the pleasure of believing before asking whether the story is true.

notice.text: Compare a refusal's emotional and practical costs.
notice.why: Saying no can express judgment, self-respect, or hope, but its price varies with money and available alternatives. The novel gives different women enough circumstances to complicate an easy ranking of their choices.

notice.text: Watch people behaving when they are not making a declaration.
notice.why: Social grace, generosity, and responsibility may become visible in how someone treats relatives, dependants, or an inconvenient obligation. An opinion formed in conversation can meet a different sort of evidence in conduct.

opening: Elizabeth Bennet hears a wealthy stranger dismiss her as not attractive enough to dance with, and finds him easy to dislike. His manners do little to change her mind. In a family where marriage can determine a woman’s future security, she takes particular pleasure in refusing to be impressed by his fortune. Austen gives Elizabeth the wit to expose other people’s absurdities, then puts her judgment to a harder test: recognising how readily she believes a story that flatters her opinion of herself.
